Gireumjang Sesame-Oil Salt Dip

Gireumjang is three ingredients and a warning that it looks like nothing: toasted sesame oil, coarse salt, and black pepper.

Korean · Easy · Makes about 80 ml (a table's bowl)

Jump to recipe ↓
Chapter 05 / 5 sauces recipes ↗

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: heritage — the purist's bowl. Gireumjang is three ingredients and a warning that it looks like nothing: toasted sesame oil, coarse salt, and black pepper. It is the dip that the unmarinated records — the classic samgyeopsal (#M10), the galbisal (#M05), the neobiani (#M08) — actually want, because it seasons without competing: the meat tastes like meat, the oil carries the salt, the pepper warms the finish. The neobiani record calls it the period-honest companion for exactly this reason. Five minutes, and the table's quietest bowl is its most important.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • The only technique is the salt's grain. Coarse salt sits in the oil and clings to the dipped meat in discrete sparks of salinity; fine salt dissolves into an oily brine that reads as one flat saltiness and over-salts fast. The dip's whole personality is the coarse grain.
  • Use genuinely toasted sesame oil (the amber, fragrant one — the same bottle the marinades run on). Cold-pressed pale sesame oil is a different ingredient entirely.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Oil in the bowl, salt and pepper over, a stir — the salt suspends, swirls, settles. That is the dish. Checkpoint — the visual: visible salt grains suspended in amber oil, pepper flecking it. Taste on a piece of the plainest grilled pork: a spark of salt, the oil's roast-nut roundness, pepper's warmth — and the meat louder for it, not quieter. That inversion is the bowl's whole argument.
  2. 02
    Serve in a shallow bowl (deep oil is a dunk hazard — a shallow pool is a touch-dip) beside the unmarinated meats, and say nothing; the table finds it. Checkpoint — by the second round of samgyeopsal, the ssamjang bowl (#SA01) and this bowl are both half-empty and the table has chosen its camps — or splits by mood, which is the usual result and the reason both bowls are set. Chef’s Note — gireumjang is the anti-sauce, and understanding why it works explains the whole dip grammar on this site: a dip's job is either to add a new voice (ssamjang, cho-gochujang) or to amplify the meat's own (this bowl, and the scallion-soy #SA04 for the shavings). The records that refuse marinades — samgyeopsal, chadolbaegi, galbisal — refuse them because their fat is the seasoning, and gireumjang is the only dip that agrees with that sentence instead of arguing with it.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Over-salty after a dip or twoFine salt usedCoarse grain; start at 3/4 tsp
Dip tastes flatOld sesame oilFresh toasted oil — the bowl has nowhere to hide
Salt settled to a crustSat too long before servingA stir before each round; it takes two seconds
Greasy mouthfeelDeep-bowl dunkingShallow bowl, touch-dip, drain the piece a beat

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Keeps 3 days refrigerated (the salt stays suspended with a stir; the oil solidifies faintly cold and re-liquefies at room temperature in minutes). Make-the-day-of is the tradition.
  • Variations: the scallion build-out for the pork records; a pinch of gochugaru for the table that cannot have an unspiced bowl; the same ratio on butter for the seafood records' (#SF12's) lane — a fusion fork, labeled as one.
